data.title: Upravnik Platform
data.excerpt: Property-management platform for residential buildings in Serbia. Building managers, board members, and residents each get their own view of the same building.
data.excerpt_xl:
Upravnik Platform is a role-based property-management system for residential buildings in Serbia. It replaces the WhatsApp group and the paper notice in the lobby with one place for announcements, forum threads, private support tickets, chat, and shared documents.

I built both halves: a NestJS/Prisma/PostgreSQL API and a Next.js/React frontend. The data model, the permission rules, and every screen are mine.

snapshot.realTime: Socket.IO chat with read receipts and automatic notifications
snapshot.apiSurface: 46 API endpoints across 13 feature areas, plus real-time chat

snapshot.soloNote: I designed the data model, wrote the permission logic, and built both the API and the frontend.

problem.lede: Residential buildings in Serbia, especially larger complexes built from several connected blocks, run informally. The manager pins a notice to the board in the lobby, residents raise problems in a WhatsApp group, and nothing records who asked for what or whether the leak ever got fixed.
body: A Complex is an optional grouping of buildings that share something physical: a courtyard, a parking structure, a boiler room. Not every building belongs to one.
A Building always belongs to at most one Complex, and owns its own units, announcements, documents, forum threads, tickets, and chat.
A Unit (apartment, office, or commercial space) belongs to exactly one Building and can be linked to at most one account, enforced at the database level, not just in application logic.

Accounts are never self-registered. There is no public sign-up. A building manager creates each resident's account and hands over the credentials, which matches how it already works, since the manager knows who lives in which apartment. A public sign-up would mean verifying that claim; this way there is nothing to verify.
problem.closing: Everything else builds on this hierarchy. Every authorization decision in the backend comes down to one question: which buildings is this user a member of, and with what role.

backend.title: Backend
backend.body: NestJS and Prisma over PostgreSQL, containerized so local and production behave the same, with JWT authentication, a real-time chat layer, and generated API docs. The validation pipe rejects any field an endpoint didn't declare, so a client can't smuggle in an extra property and overwrite something it shouldn't.

frontend.title: Frontend
frontend.body: Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Routing decides which experience you get: residents, board members, and building managers land in different app shells assembled from the same component set. Running the newest Next.js and React was a deliberate bet on the fastest-moving part of the stack.

layers.name: Identity
layers.models: One account system for everyone on the platform: admins, building managers, board members, and residents.

layers.name: Structure
layers.models: The physical hierarchy: complexes, buildings, and units.

layers.name: Membership
layers.models: Role-based access scoped to the building each person belongs to. Permissions never leak across buildings.

layers.name: Content
layers.models: Announcements and shared documents. Building-scoped, low interaction.

layers.name: Interaction
layers.models: Anything with a back-and-forth: forum threads, support tickets, cross-building discussions, and live chat.

dataModel.rolesIntro: The permission system separates who someone is from what they can do. Every person is either platform staff or a resident tied to a unit, and separately holds one role in one building: manager, board member, or resident. A handful of platform administrators sit above all of that with system-wide access. A unique constraint in the database stops anyone from holding two roles in the same building, so permissions can't go ambiguous.

authLayers.title: Platform-level access control
authLayers.body: One check that gates platform-wide operations. Creating a building or an administrator account is admin-only, and nothing further down needs to know about it.

authLayers.title: Role-based permissions
authLayers.body: A declarative guard that restricts actions by role. Only building managers and board members can post an announcement.

authLayers.title: Ownership-aware permissions
authLayers.body: The nuanced one, used in the two hardest areas of the product: support tickets and cross-building discussions. Access depends on ownership as well as role. A resident can read and reply to their own ticket; staff can act on any ticket in the building.

dataModel.callerRoleNote: The trickiest permission logic sits in the cross-building forum. A complex can span several buildings, and the same person might be a resident in one and a board member in another. The system gives them their highest role anywhere in the complex, and blocks them only if they hold no membership in any of its buildings.

businessLogic.title: Read tracking and notifications
businessLogic.body: Opening a ticket marks it read, and so does replying, without a background job or a separate tracking table. Each ticket event notifies exactly the people it should: a new ticket alerts building staff, a resident's reply alerts them again, and a staff reply goes only to the resident who opened it. Every in-app message is written in Serbian, because that is who uses this.

businessLogic.title: All-or-nothing setup
businessLogic.body: Creating a complex with its buildings and every unit runs inside one transaction. If unit 47 fails, buildings 1 through 3 don't survive either, so there is no half-built complex to clean up by hand. It exists because the admin bulk-setup wizard needed it, and the endpoint and the wizard were designed as one thing.

body: Every API change goes into the collection as it happens, with example requests, responses, required permissions, and error cases, so the frontend always has an accurate reference. A changelog tracks the same changes in order, which is the readable version of that history.

Documentation is a deliverable here. A living design document holds the mission, the account and role model, the data structure, and the order things get built in. The bulk-setup wizard got a full handoff spec covering layout, data format, and behavior before a line of it existed, which is why the two sides fit together on the first try.

The build order tells its own story. Structure first: buildings, units, accounts, roles. Then platform administration, operational details, private ticketing, read receipts, and cross-building discussions. Foundation first, product features after.

frontendDeepDive.body: The frontend splits into separate experiences per user type: residents, board members, building managers, and platform administrators. Each gets its own navigation and layout, enforced at the routing level so nobody wanders into a page meant for someone else. The same route can also render a different page depending on who is logged in. Support tickets show a building manager the full queue and a resident only their own threads. One data layer handles fetching and caching for the whole app, kept in sync with every backend change.

standoutFeature.title: Bulk Setup Wizard
standoutFeature.intro: The most elaborate thing in the frontend, and the clearest case of the API and the UI being designed together.
steps: A 3-step guided wizard: Scope, Buildings, Review. This lets an administrator set up a single building, several standalone buildings, or an entire complex in one flow.
Units can be generated automatically (by floor count and units per floor, with a choice of numbering style) or entered manually, building by building.
A CSV import mode that automatically detects whether the file describes one building, several buildings, or a full complex, and flags row-level errors before anything is submitted.
A live tree of the structure so far, so the admin can check it before committing.
One request creates the complex, its buildings, and every unit, then drops the admin on the new building list.

featureInventory.name: Secure login with role-based access for every type of user
Unified activity feed with announcements and forum posts in one place, pinned items first
Threaded discussions, both within a building and across an entire complex
Private support tickets from first message to resolution, with unread indicators
Resident and unit directory with occupancy status

designSystem.intro: The interface runs on a custom palette: teal for the brand, warm neutrals for surfaces and text, and three accents that color-code content types. Announcements, forum, chat, and documents keep their own color everywhere they appear. Type pairs a UI sans with a monospace face for numbers and timestamps.

warStory.title: The sidebar bug
warStory.body: One push shipped the ticket system, color-coded categories, and the bulk setup wizard together, and it broke the building sidebar. Expanding a building collapsed it again immediately, so you couldn't browse between buildings at all. A state reset was firing on every render instead of on a change. The fix was small: remember which building was active last, and reset the expand state only when that value changes.

scopeDeferrals.title: Real-time chat interface
scopeDeferrals.note: The backend does secure per-building messaging today. There is no chat UI yet, so that page shows a placeholder.

scopeDeferrals.title: Full document management
scopeDeferrals.note: Documents can be listed and linked. Uploading and previewing files in the app is not built.

scopeDeferrals.title: Building manager dashboard widgets
scopeDeferrals.note: Pinned content, personal to-dos, and an activity feed are planned. The page shows a preview of them for now.

backend.detail: Core data structure: accounts, complexes, buildings, units, membership, announcements, documents, forums, chat, activity logs, and notifications
Introduced a platform-level administrator role, separate from building-level roles
Added operational details like resident counts per unit
Added unread indicators for support tickets
Added discussions that span an entire complex, not just a single building

frontend.detail: One large push laying down nearly the entire app: role-based navigation for every user type, core pages, the full component library, and the data-fetching layer

A dense follow-up push that shipped the entire support-ticket system end-to-end, introduced color-coded content categories, fixed a sidebar navigation bug, added a mobile account menu, and built the full bulk setup wizard including CSV import and live preview

data.title: STK Vojvodina, Novi Sad
data.excerpt: STK Vojvodina is one of Serbia's most historic table tennis clubs, known for decades of competitive success and youth development in Novi Sad.
data.excerpt_xl:
STK Vojvodina is a table tennis club in Novi Sad, founded in the mid-20th century, with a record of competing at the top domestic level and a youth program that has run for decades.

The site collects club history, competition results, youth programs, and news into one structure the club can keep adding to without it falling apart.

Half the audience is a parent checking a result on a phone between matches; the rest are supporters and partners on a desktop. The site had to be fast and readable for both.

stats.label: Club, decades of results in one archive

It imports and exports fast-moving consumer goods: groceries, toiletries, household and laundry items, carrying brands including Coca-Cola, Mars, Jacobs, Ferrero, Red Bull, Milka, Procter & Gamble, and Unilever, alongside its own private label.
